pr_title: Signal IsCompleted from Response.BodyWriter after abort
pr_body:
# After RequestAborted, Response.BodyWriter does not signal IsCompleted/IsCanceled

<!-- Thank you for submitting a pull request to our repo. -->

<!-- If this is your first PR in the ASP.NET Core repo, please run through the checklist
below to ensure a smooth review and merge process for your PR. -->
<!-- Once all that is done, you're ready to go. Open the PR with the content below. -->
**In Progress!** - IIS fix in progress
Change logic returning FlushResult when interacting with OutputProducer to be more consistent. 
For now Changes fix only Kestrel case, with IIS I have problems debugging and can't find routine responsible for creating FlushResults


## Description

Add logic for keeping track of if output producer pending flush was canceled. Modify FlushResult returned by FlushAsync to retun IsCompleted and IsCanceled for if stream was completed and stream had pending flush canceled respectively. I implemented it on http 1 2 3 and have written tests for them. I am not sure if tests are in the correct classes so feel free to correct me here.

Fixes #32331

issue_context.title: After RequestAborted, Response.BodyWriter does not signal IsCompleted/IsCanceled

For other types of questions, consider using [StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com).

### Describe the bug
When RequestAborted occurs, code using Response.BodyWriter will not realize that the pipe is closed because **the pipe will silently discard writes** instead of signaling completion/cancellation.

Explicitly doing `BodyWriter.CancelPendingFlush()` is something of a workaround but if done after `RequestAborted` it only works under IIS Express, not when running standalone via Kestrel.

|                                              | IIS Express               | WebApp1.exe               |
|----------------------------------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| RequestAborted -> FlushResult.IsCompleted    | No                        | No                        |
| CancelPendingFlush -> FlushResult.IsCanceled | Yes                       | No                        |
| WriteAsync() after request handler returns   | ObjectDisposedException   | InvalidOperationException |

My expectation is that at minimum `.IsCompleted` is true after request is aborted. I would strongly prefer `.CancelPendingFlush()` to still also signal `.IsCanceled` in such a case.

If the request handler method ends, PipeWriter will throw `ObjectDisposedException` or `InvalidOperationException` in any case, preventing this from being a resource leak but the lack of working IsCanceled or IsCompleted signaling in this situation does complicate writing clean code because of the extra wiring needed to "manually" detect end of response in the write loop before the request handler method ends - I would much prefer to wait for the write loop to tell my request handler when it is done and use that as my signal to end the request handler.

Tested with HTTP1, though I see similar code paths also in HTTP2 and HTTP3 implementations (`if (_streamCompleted) return default;` in `FlushAsync()`).

### To Reproduce
```csharp
[HttpGet]
public async Task Get()
{
    var writeLoop = Task.Run(() => WriteLoopAsync(Response.BodyWriter));

    // CancelPendingFlush() here has no effect except when started via IIS Express.
    using var registration = HttpContext.RequestAborted.Register(() => Response.BodyWriter.CancelPendingFlush());

    await writeLoop;
}

private async Task WriteLoopAsync(PipeWriter writer)
{
    var payload = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("hello, web browser" + new string(' ', 512) + "\n");

    while (true)
    {
        var result = await writer.WriteAsync(payload);

        if (result.IsCompleted || result.IsCanceled)
        {
            // The idea is to reach this point if the body writer pipe ends (either because of RequestAborted or other reason).
            // This is not reached on RequestAborted, though. The write loop keeps "successfully" writing.
            return;
        }

        await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));
    }
}
```
